summary: In Greek mythology, Meander (Maeander, Maiandros) is the river-god of the great winding stream of Caria and Phrygia — son of Oceanus and Tethys in Hesiod's catalogue. The historical Maeander (modern Büyük Menderes) gave English the word "meander"; myth makes the god father of Cyane, who bears Byblis and Caunus to Miletus in Ovid's Milesian tale.
attribution: Adapted from Wikipedia, "Büyük Menderes River" · CC BY-SA 4.0
etymology: Ancient Greek Μαίανδρος (Maíandros); the river's bends made the name proverbial for any winding course.
symbols: reed and water attributes of river-gods

sections.heading: Genealogy
paragraphs: Hesiod names Meander among the eddying rivers Tethys bore to Oceanus, in the same breath as Eridanus, Strymon, and Alpheus. Hyginus repeats the Oceanid catalogue. As a personified stream he belongs to the divine brood of fresh waters rather than to a mortal dynasty.

Ovid and related Milesian romance make Cyane his daughter; united with Miletus she becomes mother of Byblis and Caunus. Homeric geography already pairs the Maeander with Miletus and Mycale in the Trojan Catalogue's Asian coast.

sections.heading: The famous windings
paragraphs: Ancient geographers celebrated the river's tortuous path from Celaenae toward the Aegean; its silting reshaped the Milesian gulf. A legend claimed a subterranean link with the Alpheus of Elis. In Ovid's Phaethon episode the Maeander is among the rivers that burn when the sun-chariot runs wild.
The atlas node meander is the river-god, not the modern Turkish hydronym alone.
